claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a closely related derivative has high saturation magnetization and coercivity around or below 100 Oe.
A high-pressure treatment can induce an fcc-to-hcp polymorphic transformation in an FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy.
The pressure-induced fcc-to-hcp transformation is martensitic.
The pressure-induced transformation can be controlled to produce an hcp or mixed fcc+hcp microstructure.
The pressure-induced hcp phase can be retained after recovery to ambient conditions.
High-pressure XRD studies identify pressures sufficient to initiate the fcc-to-hcp transformation.
The hcp phase has lower crystal symmetry than the fcc phase.
The hcp phase has inherently higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy than the fcc phase in the proposed alloy.
Lower symmetry and higher magnetocrystalline anisotropy increase the energy barriers for domain-wall motion.
The pressure-generated hcp or fcc+hcp structure enhances domain-wall pinning.
Enhanced magnetocrystalline anisotropy and domain-wall pinning increase the coercive field.
A pressure-induced polymorphic transformation can be performed without changing the alloy's overall composition or adding alloying elements.
Avoiding compositional modification will largely preserve the alloy's high saturation magnetization after transformation.
Both fcc and hcp CoCrFeMnNi can sustain sizable element-resolved magnetic moments in theoretical paramagnetic-state calculations.
The treatment is predicted to increase coercivity by at least 50%, and possibly several-fold, relative to the untreated fcc baseline.
The experiment will compare pressure-treated material against an untreated composition-matched single-phase fcc control at room temperature.
XRD will quantify the fcc and hcp phase fractions, while magnetic hysteresis measurements will determine coercivity and saturation magnetization.
Failure to obtain at least a 50% coercivity increase relative to the untreated control will falsify the hypothesis.
